newsitem.title: SWEDEN: SWIMMING-HACKETT WINS MEN'S 1,500 FREESTYLE WORLD TITLE.
newsitem.headline: SWIMMING-HACKETT WINS MEN'S 1,500 FREESTYLE WORLD TITLE.

text.p: Grant Hackett won the men's 1,500 metres to give Australia their ninth title of the world short-course championships in the closing race on Sunday.
Shaven-headed Hackett, bronze medallist in Friday's 400 freestyle, prevailed in an exciting duel with balding German veteran Joerg Hoffmann.
The 16-year-old Australian led for the first 400 metres but then his 27-year-old German rival moved in front before the halfway mark and edged ahead.
Hackett, however, would not let the former world long-course champion get away and hauled him in with just over 200 metres to go.
Hackett won in 14 minutes 39.54 seconds, with Hoffmann, who took silver and bronze at the first two editions of these championships, second in 14:40.67.
Bronze went to Britain's Graeme Smith, who swam 14:46.85 in a morning heat -- the programme's longest event is contested at these championships on the strength of heat times, with no final.
Olympic bronze medallist Smith had to swim in the morning session because of a slow submitted time, with his main rivals not entering the action until the evening session.
He was not allowed to swim in the fastest seeded heat, despite a British protest, because his one race of the past year in a 25-metre pool was a relatively slow 15:27.47.
Smith was not permitted to submit the 15:02.48 which earned him the Olympic bronze in Atlanta because that was achieved in a 50-metre long-course pool and he had a short-course time on record.
Fellow Briton Ian Wilson, silver medallist in 1995, was third in the evening heat but only fifth on aggregate in 14:56.29.

American Chad Carvin, who won four titles at the U.S. championships in February in his first major meet since contracting a heart virus, also had to swim in the morning and clocked 14:56.10 for fourth place overall.
Carvin, silver medallist in the 400 freestyle here, was sidelined for nearly a year after cardiomyopathy, a virus of the heart muscle, was diagnosed in December 1995 and missed the Olympics.
